title: Bishop and knight I: the W manoeuvre
summary: From the wrong corner to the right one, with the knight drawing a W.
part.corner.title: The right corner and the first points
part.corner.summary: Why mate can only be forced in the corner of the bishop's colour, and the first two points of the W.
step.t_corner: The black king is already on the edge, on h8. Before any move: in which corner can mate be forced, and which piece will take the dark squares of the eighth rank away from him?
step.t_corner.hint1: Compare the colour of h8 with the colour of your bishop's squares.
step.t_corner.hint2: The bishop never touches a dark square. The dark squares of the eighth rank belong to the other piece, jumping in a zigzag.
step.corner: De la Villa says some masters have gone home red with embarrassment for not knowing this mate. The black king is on h8, a dark square, and your bishop only moves on the light ones: this is the wrong corner. Mate exists there, but only if the defender helps; it can only be forced on a8 or h1, the corners of the bishop's colour. The journey is from h8 to a8, along the eighth rank. The knight's route, which Philidor already pointed out in 1777, draws a W: the top points, f7, d7 and b7, take the dark squares of the eighth rank; the bottom ones, e5 and c5, shut the doors d7 and b7 while the knight passes. The bishop takes the light squares and gives the final check. The first jump is 1.Nf7+.
step.d_w: The first two points of the W, in Müller and Lamprecht's line. Watch the bishop and knight take turns: the knight takes a dark square, the bishop takes the light one next to it.
step.d_w.m1: 1.Nf7+! First point. From f7 the knight takes h8 and d8, and gives check too. The black king only has g8.
step.d_w.m2: 1...Kg8, the only square: g7 belongs to your king and h7 to the bishop.
step.d_w.m3: 2.Bf5! A waiting move. 2.Bh7+? would be captured, because nothing defends h7. From f5 the bishop takes h7, and the black king only has f8.
step.d_w.m4: 2...Kf8. The king steps away from h7, and now the bishop can go there.
step.d_w.m5: 3.Bh7! Now it works: the black king is on f8, far from h7, and the bishop takes g8 for good.
step.d_w.m6: 3...Ke8, forced: e7 and g7 belong to your king.
step.d_w.m7: 4.Ne5! Second point. From e5 the knight shuts d7, the door to the centre. If the black king goes back with 4...Kf8, he loses even faster: 5.Nd7+ Ke8 6.Ke6 and both squares of the way back disappear at once.
step.d_w.m8: 4...Kd8. The black king runs to the other side, towards c8 and the seventh rank.
step.shaked: This W decided a title. Tal Shaked against Alexander Morozevich, World Junior Championship in Zagan, Poland, 1997, penultimate round. Shaked needed to win to become World Junior Champion; a draw would have cost him the title. The game reached bishop and knight against king, and Morozevich's king hid in the wrong corner. Here, on move 85, the black king is on g8, not h8. Shaked knew the way: he played the whole W, and after 95.Nc5 Morozevich resigned.
step.shaked1: You are Shaked, on move 85. The black king is on g8, not h8: here the bishop doesn't need the waiting move. Make the first two points of the W.
step.shaked1.hint: The knight first, taking h8 from the king. Then the bishop goes to the square from which it takes g8, which is now far from the black king.
step.shaked1.done: 85.Nf7, 86.Bh7 and 87.Ne5, as Shaked played. With the king already on g8, after 85.Nf7 he had to go to f8, and the bishop went straight to h7. Anna Ushenina had the position after 86...Ke8 in Geneva in 2013, on move 98, and played 98.Bf5 instead of going on with the knight: three moves slower.
part.thirdPoint.title: The third point and the bishop's wall
part.thirdPoint.summary: The black king steps out to the seventh rank, but into a box: king, knight on d7 and a quiet bishop move.
step.t_third: W line, after 4...Kd8. The black king will escape along the seventh rank, via c7, b7 and c6. Can you stop it? If not, how do you trap him there?
step.t_third.hint1: Don't try to close the seventh rank. Prepare the net for when he steps out.
step.t_third.hint2: Your king takes the squares behind him. The knight looks for the point from which it takes b6 and c5.
step.third: In the W line, after 4...Kd8, the black king steps out, but into a box. With the king on e6, you take d7 and e7. With the knight on d7, the third point of the W, you take b6 and c5. That leaves b5 and c4, and the bishop shuts them from d3, without giving check. It is a quiet move: a check would push the king out, the quiet move shuts the door and waits.
step.d_third: W line, after 4...Kd8. Watch the box close.
step.d_third.m1: 5.Ke6. The king takes d7 and e7; the black king only has c7, c8 and e8.
step.d_third.m2: 5...Kc7, the escape along the seventh rank, away from your king.
step.d_third.m3: 6.Nd7! Third point. From here the knight takes b6, b8 and c5, and your king defends it.
step.d_third.m4: 6...Kb7. The black king eyes c6 and, from there, b5 and c4.
step.d_third.m5: 7.Bd3! The quiet move. From d3 the bishop shuts b5 and c4 at once.
step.d_third.m6: 7...Kc6. The box is closed: b5, c5, b6, d5, d6 and d7 are yours. He can only go back.
step.d_third.m7: 8.Be2. It waits on the same diagonal and keeps b5 and c4; the black king only has b7 and c7.
step.d_third.m8: 8...Kc7. The black king walks back and forth inside the box.
step.d_third.m9: 9.Bf3! The bishop reaches the long diagonal, the same one as the final check on c6. From f3 it takes b7 and c6.
step.d_third.m10: 9...Kd8. Without b7 or c6, the black king goes back to the eighth rank.
step.third1: This position came up in Shaked–Morozevich, on move 89, the same as in the W line. Make the third point and, when the black king goes to b7, close the box with the bishop.
step.third1.hint: The knight goes to the point from which it takes b6 and c5. Then the bishop looks for the square that watches b5 and c4 at the same time.
step.third1.done: 89.Nd7 and 90.Bd3. If the black king steps into c6, the box is shut and he can only go back to b7 or c7. Shaked also played 89.Nd7 and 90.Bd3.
part.lastPoints.title: Push with the king, then the last points
part.lastPoints.summary: With the black king back on the eighth rank, your king pushes, the bishop shuts e8 and g8, and the knight makes c5 and b7.
step.t_last: W line, after 9...Kd8. Two points are left, c5 and b7. Before them, which piece moves, and why?
step.t_last.hint1: The knight on d7 is defended only by your king.
step.t_last.hint2: A check now gains nothing. Look for the move that takes the seventh rank away from the black king.
step.last: In the W line, after 9...Kd8, the king moves: 10.Kd6 is the only move that doesn't lose time. Your king takes c7 and e7, keeps defending the knight, and the black king is left with only c8 and e8. Push with the king, and the bishop and knight hold. Shaked did the same against Morozevich: 92.Kd6, then 93.Bd5 and 94.Bf7.
step.d_last: W line, after 9...Kd8. The king pushes, the bishop shuts the e8 side.
step.d_last.m1: 10.Kd6! The king takes c7 and e7. The black king can only move along the eighth rank.
step.d_last.m2: 10...Ke8. He tries the f8 and g8 side, far from the right corner.
step.d_last.m3: 11.Bh5+. The check drives the king off e8; f7 belongs to the bishop too.
step.d_last.m4: 11...Kd8, the only square: f8 belongs to the knight and e7 to your king.
step.d_last.m5: 12.Bf7. From f7 the bishop takes e8 and g8: the right-hand side of the eighth rank is closed.
step.d_last.m6: 12...Kc8. The black king has to head for the a8 corner.
step.last1: The same position came up in Shaked–Morozevich, on move 95. Make the last two points of the W. The knight passes through the square that shuts b7 on its way.
step.last1.hint: From d7 the knight goes to the square from which it takes b7. When the black king returns to d8, the check from b7 pushes him back.
step.last1.done: 95.Nc5 and, after 95...Kd8, 96.Nb7+. The W is complete: f7, e5, d7, c5 and b7. In the game, Morozevich resigned right after 95.Nc5, and Shaked became World Junior Champion.
part.mateB6.title: The mate in the b6 net
part.mateB6.summary: King on b6, knight on a6, bishop on c6, and a waiting bishop move so as not to stalemate.
step.t_mate: W line, after 14...Kc8. The W is over and the black king is stuck between c8 and b8. How do you mate without stalemating him?
step.t_mate.hint1: Your knight on b7 is undefended. The white king needs to come closer.
step.t_mate.hint2: In the end, the bishop gives check along the long diagonal. Before each move, count the black king's squares.
step.mateB6: In the W line, after 14...Kc8, build the b6 net: the king on b6 takes a7, b7 and c7; the knight on a6 takes b8; the bishop on c6 gives check on a8. The king comes first, and its first move, 15.Kc6, also defends the knight, which the black king could otherwise take.
step.d_mate: W line, after 14...Kc8. The white king arrives, and the knight gets close to a6.
step.d_mate.m1: 15.Kc6. The king defends the knight; the black king only has b8.
step.d_mate.m2: 15...Kb8, the only square: d8 belongs to the knight, c7 and d7 to your king.
step.d_mate.m3: 16.Kb6. The king takes a7 and c7. The black king swings between a8 and c8.
step.d_mate.m4: 16...Kc8. He runs from the corner while he can; d8 still belongs to the knight.
step.d_mate.m5: 17.Be6+. The check takes c8 and d7 from the king, and he goes back to b8.
step.d_mate.m6: 17...Kb8, the only square: d8 belongs to the knight and d7 to the bishop.
step.d_mate.m7: 18.Nc5. The knight keeps taking b7 and is one jump from a6.
step.d_mate.m8: 18...Ka8. Now the black king only has b8. A move that took b8 without giving check would be stalemate.
step.mate1: W line, after 18...Ka8. The black king only has b8. Careful: taking that square without giving check is stalemate. Finish it.
step.mate1.hint: 19.Na6?? takes b8 without check and stalemates. Wait with the bishop on a square from which it reaches c6 next move.
step.mate1.done: 19.Bd7, 20.Na6+ and 21.Bc6#. King on b6, knight on a6, bishop on c6: mate in the right corner. The waiting bishop move gave the black king the b8 square, and the knight check sent him back.
part.seirawan.title: Seirawan's wall and the c7 net
part.seirawan.summary: Another road to a8: the knight on d5 and the bishop on b5 trap the king, and the mate comes with the white king on c7.
step.t_seirawan: Seirawan's line, after 23...Kd8. The black king is on d8, out of the corner, but he can't leave this area any more. Why? And how do you take him to b8?
step.t_seirawan.hint1: Look at the squares the knight on d5 and the bishop on b5 take together.
step.t_seirawan.hint2: With the wall in place, the white king does the walking, always right next to the black king.
step.seirawan: In Seirawan's line, after 23...Kd8, this is Yasser Seirawan's wall, from his book on endings. The knight on d5 takes b6, c7 and e7; the bishop on b5 takes a6, c6, d7 and e8. The black king only has c8. Seirawan played the W up to the third point and then changed route: the bishop defended the knight, and the knight came back to the centre by another way, to d5. Now the white king pushes.
step.d_seirawan: Seirawan's line, after 23...Kd8. The wall stays put; only the white king moves.
step.d_seirawan.m1: 24.Kd6. The king takes c7 and d7; the black king only has c8.
step.d_seirawan.m2: 24...Kc8, the only square: e8 belongs to the bishop and c7 to the knight.
step.d_seirawan.m3: 25.Ke7! The king goes round the outside and takes d7 and d8. The black king goes to the b-file.
step.d_seirawan.m4: 25...Kb8. He could also go to b7; either way, he stays on the b-file.
step.d_seirawan.m5: 26.Kd8. The king takes c7 and c8 and pins the black king to the corner.
step.d_seirawan.m6: 26...Kb7. a6 and c6 belong to the bishop, b6 to the knight: the black king can't leave the box.
step.d_seirawan.m7: 27.Kd7. The king takes c6, c7 and c8.
step.d_seirawan.m8: 27...Kb8. The black king is in the a8 corner, and only the mate is left.
step.c7net: Seirawan's line, after 27...Kb8. The mate here is a different one: the c7 net. With the white king on c7, the black king is left with only a7 and a8. One piece takes one of those squares and the other gives check on the other: the bishop on b7 takes a8, and the knight gives check on a7, from c6. Mind the order: with the black king on a8, 32.Nc6?? takes a7 without check and stalemates.
step.netC7: Seirawan's line, after 27...Kb8. The mate with the king on c7. Six moves of yours: the bishop goes behind the knight, the knight heads for c6 and the king steps into c7.
step.netC7.hint: The bishop goes to c8 via a6; the knight goes to c6 via b4; the king steps into c7. The last check is a knight check.
step.netC7.done: 28.Ba6, 29.Bc8, 30.Nb4, 31.Kc7, 32.Bb7+ and 33.Nc6#. The king on c7 takes b6, b7 and b8, the bishop on b7 takes a8 and a6, and the knight gives check on a7.
part.ushenina.title: The W on the first rank
part.ushenina.summary: The W turns with the board: Ushenina against Girya, Geneva 2013, and the third point that got away.
step.t_ushenina: Anna Ushenina, women's world champion, against Olga Girya, Women's Grand Prix in Geneva, 2013. The bishop is light, the right corner is h1, and the black king, pushed along the first rank, is looking to escape to the centre before he gets there. It's your turn, in Ushenina's place, on move 82: how do you continue the W?
step.t_ushenina.hint1: The black king wants to climb the g-file, back to the centre.
step.t_ushenina.hint2: The knight has already made two points on this edge. The third one takes the g-file squares away from the black king.
step.ushenina: Girya defended well: her king ran to a1, the wrong corner, and Ushenina began the W along the first rank, from a1 to h1. It's the same W, lying on its side: c2, d4, e2, f4 and g2. The knight has already made the first two points, c2 and d4. 82.Ne2! was the third point: from e2 the knight takes g1, g3 and f4. The black king seems to get away via f3 or g2, but the bishop reins him in again on the next move. But she played 82.Bd5? The bishop takes f3 and g2, but leaves g3 free, and the black king climbs that way.
step.d_ushenina: With the bishop on d5 and the knight standing on d4, the W stopped. Watch the black king escape.
step.d_ushenina.m1: 82...Kg3. Without the knight on e2, the g-file is open, and the king climbs.
step.d_ushenina.m2: 83.Ke3. It looks like it closes things, but from here on the black king gets past the b1–h7 diagonal and the bishop can't hold him any more.
step.d_ushenina.m3: 83...Kg4. One more step towards the centre.
step.d_ushenina.m4: 84.Be4. Too late: f5 is shut, but the black king has g5 and, from there, f6.
step.d_ushenina.m5: 84...Kg5, on the way to f6 and the centre.
step.d_ushenina.m7: 85...Kf6. The black king is back in the centre, and the work starts almost from scratch.
step.ushenina1: Back to move 82. Play what Ushenina missed: the third point and, then, the bishop that stops the climb.
step.ushenina1.hint: The third point is on the second rank, next to the black king. Then the bishop shuts the way up along the c8–h3 diagonal.
step.ushenina1.done: 82.Ne2! and 83.Be6. The knight takes g1, g3 and f4, and the bishop takes g4 and h3: the black king can't get past the third rank. In the game, the third point slipped away again later, on the h-file, and Girya saved the draw by the fifty-move rule.
part.karttunen.title: The W with the dark bishop
part.karttunen.summary: With the dark-squared bishop, the right corner is h8 and the W is the mirror image: Karttunen against Rasik, 2003.
step.t_karttunen: Mika Karttunen against Vitezslav Rasik, European Club Cup, Rethymnon, Greece, 2003. Now the bishop is dark-squared. In which corner is the mate, and how does the W begin?
step.t_karttunen.hint2: The knight's first jump takes a8 from the king, like the first point in part 1, only mirrored.
step.karttunen: With the dark bishop, the right corners are a1 and h8. Rasik's king is on a8, the wrong corner, and the journey is from a8 to h8. The W is the mirror image of the one you played: c7, d5, e7, f5 and g7. Karttunen jumped exactly on those squares, from 87.Nc7+ to 99.Ng7+, and after 104.Bc5 Rasik resigned, with mate two moves away.
step.d_karttunen: Karttunen's first points. Compare with part 1: everything the same, mirrored.
step.d_karttunen.m1: 87.Nc7+! First point: the knight gives check and takes a8 from the king.
step.d_karttunen.m2: 87...Kb8, the only square: a7 belongs to the bishop and b7 to your king.
step.d_karttunen.m3: 88.Bd4. A waiting move: 88.Ba7+? would be captured. From d4 the bishop takes a7, and the black king only has c8.
step.d_karttunen.m4: 88...Kc8, the only square: a7 belongs to the bishop and a8 to the knight.
step.d_karttunen.m5: 89.Ba7! The bishop takes b8, just as 3.Bh7 took g8 in part 1.
step.d_karttunen.m6: 89...Kd8. The black king runs to the middle of the eighth rank.
step.karttunen1: Continue Karttunen's W, on move 90: the second point and, then, the king behind the black king.
step.karttunen1.hint: From d5 the knight takes c7 and e7. Then the white king takes the seventh-rank squares in front of the black king.
step.karttunen1.done: 90.Nd5 and 91.Kd6, as Karttunen played. The second point and the king that pushes: the same plan, mirrored.
step.recap: Three rules to take to your games. First: mate can only be forced in the corner of the bishop's colour; the defender runs to the other one, and the journey is along the edge. Second: the knight makes the W on any edge, the bishop shuts the squares of its own colour with quiet moves, and the king does the pushing. Third: near the corner, count the black king's squares before each move; no square and no check is stalemate.
step.playW: The whole W position. The black king on h8, the wrong corner. Take the king to a8 and mate. No hurry: the fifty-move rule is generous to those who know the way.
key.wStart: The black king hides in the wrong corner, the one the bishop can't reach. From here the W manoeuvre begins, taking it to the right corner.
key.mateCorner: Mate in the right corner: the bishop checks along the diagonal, and the knight and king take the last squares.
key.shaked: World Junior Championship 1997, in Poland: Tal Shaked had to beat Alexander Morozevich to become champion. With bishop and knight, he played the W without a slip and won the title.
key.seirawanWall: Seirawan's wall: the knight in the centre and the bishop next to it trap the black king near the right corner, even before he reaches the edge.
key.ushenina: Geneva, 2013: women's world champion Anna Ushenina missed the continuation of the W, and Olga Girya saved the draw by the fifty-move rule.
key.karttunen: European Club Cup 2003: with the dark-squared bishop, Mika Karttunen played the W mirrored, from the a8 corner to h8, and Vitezslav Rasik resigned.
history: With bishop and knight, mate can only be forced in a corner of the same colour as the bishop. A good defender runs to the other corner, the wrong one, and you need to know how to get him out. That's what the W manoeuvre is for: the knight zigzags, drawing a W on the board, while the king and bishop push the black king along the edge to the right corner. The first to call attention to this knight route was the Frenchman François-André Philidor, in 1777. The ending is rare, but it has decided a title: in 1997, Tal Shaked had to beat Alexander Morozevich with bishop and knight to become World Junior Champion, and he did. And grandmasters have lost half a point for not knowing it: Anna Ushenina, women's world champion, could only draw against Olga Girya in Geneva in 2013.
ex.e13: White to play and mate. The black king is on a7, next to the right corner, and your king already takes b8, b7 and b6. Two knight checks look possible. Which one pushes the king to a8 without opening another door?
ex.e13.hint: Look at your bishop's diagonal, from f1 to a6. One of the knight checks blocks that diagonal with its own piece.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Nc8+! forces 1...Ka8: a6 belongs to the bishop, b6 to the knight and the king, and from c8 the knight also takes a7. Then 2.Bg2 is mate along the long diagonal. The other check, 1.Nb5+, blocks the f1–a6 diagonal with the knight, and the black king escapes to a6. It is a mating net the lesson did not show: king on c7 and knight on c8, instead of king on b6 and knight on a6.
ex.e14: White to play and win. Ushenina against Girya, Geneva 2013. The black king is on a1, a dark corner, and your bishop is light-squared: the mate has to be on h1. Now the W runs along the first rank. Bring the knight to the first point. Two moves of yours.
ex.e14.hint: In the lesson, the first point took h8 from the king. Here the square to take is a1, and from d1 the knight cannot get there in one jump: it needs a stepping stone.
ex.e14.solution: 77.Ne3! Kb1 78.Nc2, as Ushenina played. From c2 the knight takes a1 and e1, the dark edge squares near the black king: it is the first point of the W, the same idea as 1.Nf7 in the lesson, now on the first rank. She went on with 79.Ba2, which takes b1 as 2.Bh7 took g8, and 80.Nd4, the second point. The stumble came later.
ex.e15: White to play and win. The knight on b8 is attacked by the black king, and mate is close. Only one move wins: save the knight without stalemating the king.
ex.e15.hint: If the knight leaves b8, the black king has no move. If the bishop moves, the knight falls, and king and bishop cannot mate. One piece is left to move.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kc7! defends the knight and gives a7 back to the black king. After 1...Ka7, 2.Bc8! takes the bishop behind the knight, 2...Ka8, 3.Bb7+ Ka7 and 4.Nc6 is mate: the king on c7 takes b8, b7 and b6, the bishop on b7 is protected by the king and takes a8, and the knight gives the check. 1.Nc6 or 1.Nd7 on the first move stalemate the black king, and any other move lets the knight fall.
ex.e17: White to play and win. Karttunen against Rasik, European Club Cup, 2003. The bishop is dark-squared and the mate will be on h8. The W was going well, but the black king slipped off the edge to f6. Send the king back to the eighth rank and squeeze him again. Three moves of yours.
ex.e17.hint: A bishop check now lets the black king go down to g5. First close the squares on the way down with a quiet bishop move; then the bishop returns to the long diagonal. When the black king is back on the eighth rank, choose: squeeze with the king or with the bishop?
ex.e17.solution: 93.Be3! takes g5 and f4; the knight on e7 already takes f5 and g6, and your king takes e5 and e6. The black king has to go back: 93...Kf7. Then 94.Bd4 (94.Bg5, 94.Bf4 and 94.Kd7 also work) closes the road again, and the black king returns to the eighth rank: 94...Ke8. Now 95.Ke6!, with the king and not the bishop: your king takes d7 and f7, and the black king can only walk along the eighth rank. Karttunen played all three moves. The check 93.Bd4+ on the first move looks more natural, but lets the king go to g5; and 95.Bb6 on the last one, defending the knight, also takes longer.
ex.e18: White to play and win. Another road after the third point of the W, from Seirawan's line quoted on Wikipedia: black king on c7, knight on d7, bishop on c4. Lock the king in the a8 corner without the W to b7. Three moves of yours.
ex.e18.hint: The knight on d7 is attacked and only your king defends it. Give it a second defender that also takes c6 from the black king. Then the knight finds, by another road, the central square from which it takes b6 and c7 at once.
ex.e18.solution: 1.Bb5! defends the knight and takes c6 and a6 (1.Bd5 also works, a little slower). After 1...Kd8, the knight leaves d7 (2.Nf6, as Seirawan played; 2.Nc5, 2.Ne5 and 2.Nb6 come to the same; 2.Kd6 also wins) and, when the king returns to c7, 3.Nd5+ sends him back to the eighth rank: from d5 the knight takes b6, c7 and e7. The black king is locked in the a8 corner, and the white king comes closer for the mate.
ex.e19: White to play and win. Ushenina against Girya, Geneva 2013, later on. The black king went towards the wrong corner, h8, and now the W runs down the h-file, to h1, your bishop's corner. Five moves of yours; the last one is the move the world champion missed.
ex.e19.hint: Start with the bishop: seal the black king behind the a2–g8 diagonal and then the bishop takes from the king the light square on the h-file he still has. The knight returns to the centre and the king follows. At the end, the black king wants to get out through f2 and e3: one knight jump closes both.
ex.e19.solution: 103.Be6! Kh6, 104.Bg8! Kh5 (the bishop takes h7 and holds the a2–g8 diagonal), 105.Ne5 Kh4 (the knight takes g4 and g6), 106.Kf5 (or a waiting bishop move, 106.Bd5 or 106.Bb3) 106...Kg3 and 107.Ng4! The knight takes f2, e3 and h2, and the black king is locked in the h1 corner. In the game, Ushenina played 107.Bc4? instead of 107.Ng4, the black king escaped through f2 and the game ended in a draw by the fifty-move rule. 107.Bb3 also wins, only more slowly.
practice: Now the real endgame. In this position the black king is near h1, the right corner for your bishop: close the net and mate without stalemating. Pick a pace and challenge the clock, or set up your own training.
